label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
**4 stars.** I'll explain what's missing so you don't have to ask.

We bought the PT-20 from Chancel AV in February 2026 ($2,140, plus $95 for the wall mount) to replace the webcam we'd been livestreaming with since 2020. We run it into OBS on the old office PC, out to our YouTube channel, usually 30–60 viewers on a Sunday. The single PoE cable up to the balcony was the thing that sold me — one line, no power run, no mess. Whoever is considering this: the install was simpler than the price suggested.

**Setup.** Our nave is 92 feet long and the camera is on the balcony rail at the back, so we're working with the zoom to reach the chancel. 20x optical gets us there with usable framing; I won't pretend it's pixel-peeping at the far wall, but the faces at the pulpit are clearly good enough for people to watch a service on their phone or laptop. We have nine presets stored — altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide shot, and two for the chancel steps. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, runs it from the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon. That matters more to me than any spec sheet: he's not an engineer and neither am I, and we didn't need a consultant or a manual to figure out the controls.

**The one real problem.** The first Sunday, the presets had drifted a few degrees by the time we got to the sermon, so the camera was pointing at the wall beside the pulpit. Chancel AV's support — Marcy — was excellent on the phone and got the firmware update (2.4, in March) pointed at us. That fixed it. We've had no drift since.

**Picture quality.** Fine in normal service light. The honest test was the Easter Vigil in April, our first "Christ the Lord Is Risen Today" with only candles and no house lights up. The picture got grainy, noticeably so. It stayed usable — we could see the paschal candle, the people around it, the words on the screen. The old webcam, in the same service, showed nothing but dots. If your church does candlelight, know that this is a low-light camera, not a night vision camera. It will carry you, with grain.

**Autofocus hunts** when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit. We lock focus on the presets and leave it alone. That's the fix, and it works.

**Two complaints.** The manual is thin and badly translated. Call the support line. And the audio is not the camera's job and it did nothing for our sound problem — we still fight our sound system every Sunday, and no camera will fix that. If your issue is audio, don't buy this expecting it to help.

**Who should buy this.** A church our size or larger, with a balcony or side mount and someone comfortable running a browser. We would buy it again. But a congregation under 100 people might do fine with something cheaper and put the difference toward better microphones, which I think is the better buy for most of us. We spent good money on a camera and still have a sound system that needs attention.

The other thing I'd say: Delores, who's 82 and homebound, called me afterward to say she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That's what we bought it for.
